At Longines, a Single Digit Separates a Chronometer From Its Cheaper Twin
The HydroConquest dive watch runs on essentially the same movement as the brand's chronometer-certified Spirit line. Skipping one costly Swiss test may save buyers in Thailand 20,000 baht or more.
LONGINES HydroConquest 2026. THE SIAM TIMES.

For most shoppers, the reference number on a watch movement is fine print. At Longines, the Swiss watchmaker founded in 1832 and now owned by the Swatch Group, the digit after the decimal point says a great deal about what a customer is paying for.

A caliber ending in 4, like the L888.4 inside the Spirit collection, has been tested and certified as a chronometer by the Swiss Official Chronometer Testing Institute, known by its French acronym, COSC. A caliber ending in 5 shares the same construction and high-grade materials but never undergoes the test. That is the family Longines chose for its HydroConquest dive watches.

The HydroConquest, a fixture of the brand's dive-watch lineup since 2007, was thoroughly overhauled this year in 39- and 42-millimeter sizes and remains water-resistant to 300 meters, or nearly 1,000 feet. Its three-hand models run on the L888.5, an automatic caliber that ETA, a Swatch Group sister company, builds for Longines alone. The movement stores 72 hours of power, enough to keep running for three days off the wrist, and uses a silicon balance spring, the hair-thin coil that governs a watch's rate. It is rated to resist magnetic fields 10 times stronger than the ISO standard requires.

The L888.5 is a standard, no-nonsense movement built for durability and simplicity, and it includes a quickset date, which lets the wearer advance the date directly from the crown. The HydroConquest GMT does without that convenience, for reasons rooted in its design. Its L844.5 caliber was conceived from the outset as a so-called true GMT, with a local hour hand that can be reset on its own, in one-hour jumps, while home time stays put. Because the date is linked to that hand, correcting it means turning the hour hand forward or backward past midnight, one midnight at a time, until the right date appears — the same arrangement found in travel watches like Rolex's GMT-Master II.

Introduced in 2023, the GMT was the first in the collection's history, though the brand's experience with dual-time wristwatches stretches back to 1925. Its movement is, for practical purposes, the L844.4 found in the Spirit Zulu Time; the chief difference is that the Spirit version carries COSC certification.

That certificate is no formality. COSC examines movements rather than finished watches, testing each one individually for 15 days, in five positions and at three temperatures. To pass, a movement must stay within an average of four seconds slow or six seconds fast per day. Only about 3 percent of Swiss watches carry the designation, according to the trade publication Europa Star.

Putting every movement through that regimen costs money and adds weeks to production. By fitting the HydroConquest with .5 calibers, Longines sidesteps both and can price the watch aggressively, a shrewd bit of cost control that still leaves buyers with premium hardware like the silicon hairspring. Silicon is unaffected by magnetism and stands up well to corrosion and wear; because it is lighter and harder than steel, it also reduces inertia, and it needs no oil.

The math shows up at the register. In Thailand, the HydroConquest sells for roughly 60,000 to 70,000 baht, or about $1,800 to $2,100. Certifying every piece could push that to 80,000 to 90,000 baht or more — about $2,400 to $2,700 — eroding its edge among dive watches in that price range.

A higher price would also push the HydroConquest into the territory of the brand's own Spirit line, whose central selling point is chronometer precision. Introduced in 2020 as a tribute to 20th-century aviators and adventurers, the Spirit collection is built around certified chronometer movements, and its dials carry five stars, reviving an old Longines custom of grading its finest calibers by star count.

Under the dial, the HydroConquest and the Spirit have more in common than their price tags suggest. What separates their movements is a certificate, and the 15 days in a Swiss laboratory it takes to earn one.
